introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.p: Personal names are among the most commonly exchanged information on the Internet. However, the detail of personal names during interchange often recedes to the lowest common denominator understood by both sides, which is a plain string.

Such exchange invariably entails the loss of most semantic structure of a personal name, causing a range off issues from inappropriate greetings at hotels to failure of name verification at national borders.
This International Standard facilitates the interchange and interaction of names between humans and applications without loss of fidelity.

This standard addresses the structure of personal names in ISO standards covering topics such as bibliographic management, personal identification documents, electronic messaging, e-commerce to postal applications.

clause.title: Scope
clause.p: This document specifies a reference model for “personal names”, suitable for machine encoding, for digital storage and transmission.
The reference model is composed of the following data elements:

li.p: cultural name profiles for personal name patterns; and
template definitions for the display and input of personal names.

clause.p: This document does not handle the linkage of a personal name to an identity.
The personal name model is used to encode a person’s personal names for:

li.p: as an interoperable data structure used with databases

clause.p: The cultural name profile model is used to guide rendering of a name model instance as a string as appropriate to the applied cultural name profile.

clause.title: Data types
clause.p: These are the basic data types used in this document.

dd.p: Container for URIs, as defined by .
Code for language or language family, as specified in . The specification is open as to whether the two-letter code or the three-letter code for languages is used.
Code for scripts (writing scripts), as specified in .
String which optionally specifies its language and/or script.

clause.title: General
clause.p: A personal name is composed of multiple components. Personal names are modelled with the cultural origin and information provided within a personal name in mind.
A personal name is represented by the following model.

clause.title: Modelling
clause.p: Names are modelled in constituent components or as a complete name string.
The initials component is used if all forenames are replaced by initials. If only the middle name is replaced by an initial, it is still treated as a forename.

clause.title: Pseudonyms and variant names
clause.p: Variant names, and assumed names, can both be modelled as names.

clause.title: Anonymous
clause.p: A representation of an intentionally anonymous personal name.

clause.title: Unknown
clause.p: A representation of an unknown personal name.

clause.title: Varii
clause.p: Descriptors of individuals, such as “Various Authors”, should be given as completeName elements.
As with pseudonyms, the real name of the creator if known can be modelled as a note, or as a name variant.

clause.title: Pseudonym
clause.p: A pseudonym or alias is a name that a person or group assumes for a particular purpose, which can differ from their given name(s).

clause.title: General
clause.p: The family name is the portion of a personal name that indicates a person’s family (or tribe or community, depending on the culture).

Depending on the culture, all members of a family unit may have identical family names or there may be variations based on the cultural rules.
Not all cultures provide a family name in a personal name.

clause.title: Compound family name
clause.p: A compound family name is one based on merged family names.

clause.title: Patrilineal family name
clause.p: A patrilineal family name is a name originated from the family name of the father.

clause.title: Matrilineal family name
clause.p: A matrilineal family name is a name originated from the family name of the mother.

clause.title: Matronymic

example.sourcecode: An example TEI representation of a personal name with a matronymic family name<persName> <surname type="matronymic">FitzEmpress</surname>, <forename>Henry</forename> </persName>

clause.p: A matronymic name is a name originated from one of the name components of the mother or a matrilineal ancestor.
Different cultures have different ways of producing matronymic family names.

clause.title: Patronymic
clause.p: A patronymic name is a name originated from one of the name components of the father or a patrilineal ancestor.
Different cultures have different ways of producing patronymic family names.

example.p: Mongolian: Otryadyn Gündegmaa, O. Gündegmaa, Otryadyn is the patronymic family name

clause.title: Genonymic
clause.p: A genonymic name is a name derived from one of the name components of an ancestor.

note.p: the genonymic could come from a parent, grandparent or an earlier ancestor.

clause.title: Avonymic
clause.p: An avonymic name is a name derived from one of the name components of a grandfather.

clause.title: Paedonymic
clause.p: An paedonymic name is a name derived from one of the name components of a child.

clause.title: Religious name
clause.p: A religious name is a name or title given to, or used by, a person according to the tradition of the person’s religion.

clause.title: Title
clause.p: A title is a name that describes a position or job.

clause.title: Maiden name
clause.p: A maiden name is a family name that a married woman used prior to its being changed at marriage.

clause.title: Mononymous
clause.p: Some personal names are known and addressed by a single given name.

In some areas of the world, many people are known by a single name, and so are said to be mononymous.
Mononymic name is considered as a given name without a family name.

example.p: Thant, third Secretary-General of the United Nations.

clause.title: Given name
clause.p: Diagram of naming conventions, using John Fitzgerald Kennedy as an example.
The sarcophagus of Queen Desideria at Riddarholm Church in Sweden. The name was given to Desideria Clary not at birth but when she was created Crown Princess of Sweden in 1810.
A given name is usually is given to a person, normally to a child by his or her parents at or close to the time of birth.

By contrast, a family name (also known as a family name, last name, or gentile name), which is normally inherited, is typically shared with other members of one’s immediate family. Regnal names and religious or monastic names are special given names bestowed upon someone receiving a crown or entering a religious order. Such a person then typically becomes known chiefly by that name.
There could be more than one given name in a personal name.

clause.title: middle name
clause.p: A middle name is a given name in some cultures that is not a first name or a family name.

clause.title: Arabic name
clause.p: Arabic names were historically based on a long naming system; most Arabs did not have given/middle/family names, but a full chain of names. This system was mainly in use throughout the Arab world.

li.p: Ism, given name, first name or personal name
Laqab, family name, nickname, title, honorific
Kunya, teknonym (name of first son or daughter) or nickname

clause.title: Christian name, baptismal name, confirmation name

example.p: The baptised name of “Sun Yat-sen”, the father of modern China, is “Yat Sun” (日新).

clause.title: Papal name
clause.p: A papal name or pontificial name is the regnal name taken by a pope.
Both the head of the Catholic Church, usually known as the Pope, and the Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria (Coptic Pope) choose papal names.

example.p: John Paul II.
Tawadros II
Jose Maria Rodrigues Jr.
King George VI

clause.title: Nickname
clause.p: A nickname is a familiar name given to a person instead of or as well as the real personal name.

example.p: The given name “Mikhail” in Russion often goes by the nickname “Misha”.
The given name “José” in Spanish often goes by the nickname “Pepe”.
The given name “William” in English often goes by the nickname “Bill”.

clause.title: General
clause.p: A style of office or honorific is an official or legally recognized title.
An honorific is a title that conveys esteem or respect for position or rank when used in addressing or referring to a person.
Different types of honorific:

note.p: Bibliographic entries often encounter this problem of separation of name and honorifics.

example.p: Doctor, Dr.

clause.title: Royal
clause.p: Titles and styles

li.p: 4 August 1900 – 16 February 1904: The Honourable Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon
26 April 1923 – 11 December 1936: Her Royal Highness The Duchess of York
11 December 1936 – 6 February 1952: Her Majesty The Queen
11 December 1936 – 14 August 1947 (for British India): Her Imperial Majesty The Queen-Empress
6 February 1952 – 30 March 2002: Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother

figure.name: An example of names with honorific presented in terms of class instantiations.

clause.title: Style of office
clause.p: A style of office is an official or legally recognized title.
Such styles are associated with monarchies, presidents, members of legislative bodies, judges, office holders and religious figures.

example.p: “Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam”, former President of India, styled as “His Excellency Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam”.
“The Honorable Ruth Bader Ginsburg” in the United States.
“His Honour Judge Michael Wong” in Hong Kong.
Esquire as a social rank in UK (lawyer in US)
Ex-President

clause.title: Honors
clause.p: Orders of chivalry confer titles to its holders.

example.p: The Most Excellent Order of the British Empire is a British order of chivalry, conferring appointments to classes including: “Knight Grand Cross or Dame Grand Cross of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (GBE)”, “Knight Commander or Dame Commander of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (KBE or DBE)”, “Commander of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (CBE)”, “Officer of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (OBE)” and “Member of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire (MBE)”.
“Sir Hugh Beach, GBE KCB MC”.

clause.title: General
clause.p: Personal name order depends on the cultural profile of the name.

example.p: The name order of “[given name(s)] [family name]” is commonly used throughout most European countries.

The name order of “[family name] [given name(s)]” is commonly used in East Asia (for example in China, Japan, Korea, Malaysian Chinese, Singapore, and Vietnam, among others), as well as in Southern and North-Eastern parts of India, and in Hungary.
The name order of “[given name(s)] [father’s family name] [mother’s family name]” is commonly used in Spanish-speaking countries such as Spain and Uruguay.

clause.title: Abbreviation
clause.p: The abbreviated forms of a personal name has the following two aspects:

li.p: as a way of presentation, as derived from a non-abbreviated form; and
as a characterization of data representing the name.
In other words, the source of the name is already in an abbreviated form.

example.p: “Pablo Diego José Francisco de Paula Juan Nepomuceno María de los Remedios Cipriano de la Santísima Trinidad Ruiz y Picasso” becomes “Pablo Ruiz y Picasso”.
Ll. George” for (British prime minister) David Lloyd George.

clause.title: Name concerns
clause.p: In the rendering of a personal name, the following concerns are important.

li.p: If the personal name is made to fit into a shorter string length, which elements should remain.

example.p: “Pablo Diego José Francisco de Paula Juan Nepomuceno María de los Remedios Cipriano de la Santísima Trinidad Ruiz y Picasso” becomes “Pablo Ruiz y Picasso”.

li.p: If a personal name is made to fit into a short length, how to render an appropriate, abbreviated name.

example.p: “Avul Pakir Jainulabdeen Abdul Kalam”, former President of India, is abbreviated as “A. P. J. Abdul Kalam”.

clause.title: Chinese
clause.p: Chinese personal names are names used by those from mainland China, Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, and the Chinese diaspora overseas.
Chinese names consist of a family name (姓, xìng), followed by a given name (名, míng).

clause.title: English
clause.p: name components:

English names are names used in, or originating in, England. In England as elsewhere in the English-speaking world, a complete name usually consists of a given name, commonly referred to as a first name or Christian name, and a (most commonly patrilineal) family name or surname, also referred to as a last name.
There can be several given names, some of these being often referred to as a second name, or middle name(s).
Double-barrelled names, compound surnames in English feature two words, are often joined by a hyphen or hyphens.

example.p: Henry Hepburne-Scott
Some families having as many as three or four words making up their surname.
Charles Hepburn-Stuart-Forbes-Trefusis, 21st Baron Clinton.
It is not unusual for compound surnames to be composed of separate words not linked by a hyphen.

clause.title: French
clause.p: name components:
French people have one, two or more given names (first names). One of them is used in daily life.

clause.title: Examples

example.p: “Jacques Chirac” instead of officially of Jacques René Chirac.
“Philippe Pétain” instead of officially of Henri Philippe Pétain, because Philippe was the given name that he used in daily life.

clause.p: Middle names in the English sense do not exist, and middle initials are never used for second or further given names.

example.p: Claude Allègre may be cited as “Claude J. Allègre” in English-speaking scientific publications, but not in French ones.

clause.title: German
clause.p: name components:
Personal names in German-speaking Europe consist of one or several given names (Vorname, plural Vornamen) and a surname (Nachname, Familienname). The Vorname is usually gender-specific.

clause.title: Examples

example.p: Otto Eduard Leopold Fürst von Bismarck.

clause.p: The Vorname (in English forename) is usually given to a child by the parents shortly after birth. It is common to give a child several Vornamen (forenames).
The Rufname (“appellation name” or “call name”) is the given name intended for everyday use, and is often underlined on official documents.

example.p: The Rufname of the mathematician Amalie Emmy Noether is “Emmy”.

clause.title: Hungarian
clause.p: name components:

example.p: Kovács János
If there is more than one given name, they come in order of importance after the family name:
There can be more than one family name, which can be written fully or abbreviated into initials:

clause.title: Icelandic
clause.p: name components:

Icelandic names differ from most current Western family name systems by being patronymic or occasionally matronymic: they indicate the father (or mother) of the child and not the historic family lineage.
Iceland’s traditional name system was formerly used by all Nordic countries except partly Finland.

The Icelandic system is not based on family names (although some people do have family names and might use both systems). Generally, a person’s second name indicates the first name of their father (patronymic) or in some cases mother (matronymic). According to Icelandic naming tradition, second names end in -son or -dóttir with few exceptions.

clause.title: Examples

example.p: Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir. “Jóhanna, daughter of Sigurður”.
Matronymic. Heiðar Helguson, “Helguson, son of Helga”.
Örvar Þóreyjarson Smárason. (Örvar, son of Þórey, son of Smári)

clause.p: Some family names do exist in Iceland, most commonly adaptations from last name patronyms Icelanders took up when living abroad.

example.p: Geir Haarde, Eiður Smári Guðjohnsen, Anita Briem.
Nobel Prize-winning author Halldór Laxness, born as Halldór Guðjónsson.

clause.title: Indonesian
clause.p: name components:
Indonesians generally use given names without a family name. The majority of Indonesians do not have family names. Rather, their given names are geographically and culturally specific.
Some given names include a family name or a patronymic.

clause.title: Typical name patterns
clause.p: Indonesian names usually fall into one of the following categories:

li.p: Polynymic names without a family name
Polynymic names with a family name

clause.p: An Indonesian name is often mis-represented in other cultures, such as:

li.p: Netherlands: the word “Onbekend” (“unknown”) is assigned as a last name
Germany: the one-word name is used as both given name and surname
US: “Fnu” (family name unknown) is assigned as the first or given name, “Lnu” (last name unknown) is assigned as the family, surname or last name, or the name is duplicated as the surname.

example.p: “Mulyono”, the original name of “Joko Widodo.”
Kusno Sosrodihardjo
Fransiskus Xaverius Hadi Rudyatmo
Sudono Salim

clause.title: Italian
clause.p: A name in Italian consists of a given name (nome) and a surname (cognome). Surnames are normally written after given names.

clause.title: Japanese
clause.p: Japanese names usually consist of a family name (surname), followed by a given name.
name components:

Japanese names are usually written in kanji, where characters are logographic, but each with a variety of possible Japanese pronunciations. Therefore often names cannot in general be spelled or pronounced unless both the spelling and pronunciation are given.

example.p: 大翔 is traditionally pronounced “Hiroto”, but can also be pronounced as “Haruto”, “Yamato”, “Taiga”, “Sora”, “Taito”, “Daito”, and “Masato”.
大和 can be read as Daiwa or Yamato.
東海林 can be read as Tōkairin or Shōji
“中山樵” (Nakayama Sho), the Japanese pseudonym of “Sun Yat-sen”:

clause.title: Jewish
clause.p: name components:
Modern Jewish names include Hebrew patronymic names as well as family names.

clause.title: Korean
clause.p: name components:
A Korean name consists of a family name followed by a given name, as used by the Korean people in both South Korea and North Korea.
In the Korean language, ireum or seongmyeong usually refers to the family name (seong) and given name (myeong) together.

clause.title: Manchu
clause.p: name components:
Manchus are called only by their given names. Manchu clan names (“hala”) are not used with their personal names, but occasionally a family name is used.

example.p: “Tulišen”
“Hiowan Ye” (玄烨)
“Aisin-Gioro Ulhicun”, linguist. The family name is “Aisin-Gioro”.

clause.title: Mongolian
clause.p: name components:
Mongolian names traditionally consists of only one personal name.

example.p: Отрядын Гүндэгмаа (“Otryadyn Gündegmaa”), a Mongolian shooter, has “Otryadyn” as a patronym, “Gündegmaa” as given name.
Халтмаагийн Баттулга (“Khaltmaagiin Battulga”), President of Mongolia.

clause.title: Portuguese
clause.p: name components:
Portuguese often have two personal names, although the first may at times be used on its own.

example.p: George Agostinho Baptista da Silva
“António Caetano de Abreu Freire Egas Moniz”, Nobel prize winner. He was the child of “Fernando de Pina Rezende Abreu” and “Maria do Rosario de Almeida e Sousa”.

clause.title: Slavic
clause.p: name components:
Slavic naming applies to Russian, Ukrainian, Belorussian, Bulgaria, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Macedonia, as well as some populations of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan.

example.p: Ива́н Константи́нович Айвазо́вский (“Ivan Konstantinovich Aivazovsky”). Ivan is the given name, Konstantinovich the patronymic name, Aivazovsky the family name.
Олександр Іванович Білаш, (“Oleksandr Ivanovych Bilash”). Oleksandr is the given name, Ivanovych the patronymic name, Bilash the family name.

clause.title: Spanish
clause.p: name components:

example.p: Salvador de Madariaga y Rojo, Spanish diplomat, writer, historian and pacifist. Child of Darío José de Madariaga​ and María Ascensión Rojo.

clause.title: Thai
clause.p: name components:
Modern Thai names are composed of given names followed by the family name. Prior to 1913, family names were not required.

example.p: ชวน หลีกภัย (“Chuan Likphai”)

clause.title: Vietnamese
clause.p: name components:
Vietnamese personal names are names used by those from Vietnam and the Vietnamese diaspora overseas.
Vietnamese names consist of a family name (Tên, 𠸛), followed by a given name (Họ, /𢩜). Between the family name and given name, one or more additional names may be present.
Vietnamese additional names can be a middle name (tên đệm), generational name, or clan distinguisher name. The middle name, for identification purposes, can be omitted.
Courtesy names are also allowed, separate from the given name.

bibitem.abstract: This part of ISO 639 provides a code consisting of language code elements comprising two-letter language identifiers for the representation of names of languages. The language identifiers according to this part of ISO 639 were devised originally for use in terminology, lexicography and linguistics, but may be adopted for any application requiring the expression of language in two-letter coded form, especially in computerized systems. The alpha-2 code was devised for practical use for most of the major languages of the world that are not only most frequently represented in the total body of the world’s literature, but which also comprise a considerable volume of specialized languages and terminologies. Additional language identifiers are created when it becomes apparent that a significant body of documentation written in specialized languages and terminologies exists. Languages designed exclusively for machine use, such as computer-programming languages, are not included in this code.

La présente partie de l’ISO 639 fournit un code composé de codets de langue formés avec des indicatifs de langue à deux lettres pour la représentation des noms de langue. Les indicatifs de langue figurant dans la présente partie de l’ISO 639 ont été conçus principalement pour être utilisés en terminologie, lexicographie et linguistique mais peuvent être adaptés à toute autre application dans laquelle il est nécessaire d’exprimer une langue sous la forme d’un code à deux lettres, notamment dans le cadre des systèmes informatiques. Le code alpha-2 a été créé pour un usage pratique pour la plupart des grandes langues du monde qui ne sont pas seulement les plus souvent représentées dans le corpus de la littérature mondiale, mais pour lesquelles il existe également un volume considérable de langues de spécialité et de terminologies. De nouveaux indicatifs de langue sont créés lorsqu’il devient évident qu’il existe un corpus significatif de documentation écrite dans des langues de spécialité et des terminologies. Les langages créés pour être utilisés exclusivement par des machines, comme les langages de programmation, ne sont pas inclus dans le présent code.

bibitem.abstract: ISO 15924:2004 provides a code for the presentation of names of scripts. The codes were devised for use in terminology, lexicography, bibliography and linguistics, but they may be used for any application requiring the expression of scripts in coded form. ISO 15924:2004 also includes guidance on the use of script codes in some of these applications.

bibitem.abstract: ISO 639-3:2007 provides a code, published by the Registration Authority of ISO 639-3, consisting of language code elements comprising three-letter language identifiers for the representation of languages. The language identifiers according to this ISO 639-3:2007 were devised for use in a wide range of applications, especially in computer systems, where there is potential need to support a large number of the languages that are known to have ever existed. Whereas ISO 639-1 and ISO 639-2 are intended to focus on the major languages of the world that are most frequently represented in the total body of the world’s literature, ISO 639-3:2007 attempts to provide as complete an enumeration of languages as possible, including living, extinct, ancient and constructed languages, whether major or minor, written or unwritten. As a result, ISO 639-3:2007 deals with a very large number of lesser-known languages. Languages designed exclusively for machine use, such as computer-programming languages and reconstructed languages, are not included in this code.

L’ISO 639-3:2007 fournit un code, publié par l’Agence d’enregistrement de l’ISO 639-3, composé de codets de langue formés avec des indicatifs de langue à trois lettres pour la représentation des langues. Les indicatifs de langue de l’ISO 639-3:2007 ont été conçus pour être utilisés dans une large gamme d’applications, en particulier dans les systèmes informatiques, lorsqu’il y a un besoin potentiel de prise en charge du grand nombre de langues dont l’existence est connue. Alors que l’ISO 639-1 et l’ISO 639-2 se focalisent sur les grandes langues du monde les plus fréquemment représentées dans le corpus de la littérature mondiale, l’ISO 639-3:2007 vise à fournir une énumération de langues la plus complète possible, y compris les langues vivantes, les langues mortes, les langues anciennes et les langues construites artificiellement, qu’elles soient majeures ou mineures, écrites ou orales. Par conséquent, l’ISO 639-3:2007 traite d’un très grand nombre de langues moins connues. Les langages créés pour être exclusivement utilisés dans des machines, comme les langages de programmation, ainsi que les langues reconstituées ne sont pas inclus dans le présent code.

bibitem.title: Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax
bibitem.abstract: A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is a compact sequence of characters that identifies an abstract or physical resource. This specification defines the generic URI syntax and a process for resolving URI references that might be in relative form, along with guidelines and security considerations for the use of URIs on the Internet. The URI syntax defines a grammar that is a superset of all valid URIs, allowing an implementation to parse the common components of a URI reference without knowing the scheme-specific requirements of every possible identifier. This specification does not define a generative grammar for URIs; that task is performed by the individual specifications of each URI scheme. [STANDARDS-TRACK]
